stops.name: Alexandria, the fifty philosophers converted and burned
stops.campa: The emperor gathers fifty orators and philosophers, the masters of Egypt, to break one girl in argument. She converts them instead: hearing her expound the Incarnation out of their own Sibyls and Plato, the fifty confess Christ together. Maxentius burns them in the midst of the city, and the fire, the canon is exact, consumes neither hair nor garment; the bodies lie whole as sleepers. Fifty philosophers led to God by a virgin of Alexandria: the school of Hypatia, says the fold, refounded in heaven.

stops.name: Alexandria, the prison: the dove and the empress
stops.campa: Twelve days she lies in a darkened cell without food, and a dove of heaven feeds her, and Christ visits her with light. The empress Faustina comes secretly by night with Porphyrius the captain and two hundred knights to see the prisoner; they find the cell shining and angels anointing her wounds, and all are converted on the spot. The emperor will kill his own wife and his own general before he touches the girl; the story insists on it: her prison converts the palace faster than his palace can empty her prison.

stops.name: Alexandria, the wheel that shatters
stops.campa: The provost Cursates builds the engine: four wheels bound with iron saws and sharp nails, two turning against two, that the virgin may be torn apart as a terror to the city. Katherine prays. An angel of the Lord strikes the machine, and the wheel bursts asunder at her touch with such violence that four thousand of the heathen are slain by its flying wreckage. The instrument becomes her signature: forever after she is known by the broken wheel: the sign that the engines of the world do not survive contact with wisdom.

stops.name: Alexandria, the beheading: milk, not blood
stops.campa: Led out to the place of execution, she prays that whoever remembers her passion may be heard, and a voice answers from heaven: Come, my love, my spouse; the door of heaven is opened to thee. The sword falls, and from her body issues milk instead of blood, the sign the canon sets against the tiles of the Caesareum: where the philosopher was opened with shells and gave blood, the saint is opened with steel and gives milk, the drink of teachers, the first food of the soul. Alexandria has killed its wise virgin twice; this time the body will not stay for the fire.

stops.name: Mount Sinai, Jebel Katherina: the angels lay down the body
stops.campa: Angels take up the body from the killing ground of Alexandria and bear it through the air more than twenty days' journey, to the highest mountain of Sinai, the peak beside the mountain of the Law, and bury it there with honor. The geometry is deliberate: from the city of the murdered philosopher to the mountain where God spoke definitions out of fire. What Cinaron's flames were denied, Sinai's granite receives. The mountain takes her name; from her bones, continually, runs an oil that heals all sickness.

stops.name: Mount Sinai, Justinian's fortress-monastery at the Burning Bush
stops.campa: The emperor Justinian walls in the Burning Bush at the mountain's foot: a fortress-church garrisoned with monks, the oldest continuously inhabited monastery in Christendom, its library second only to Rome's. Prophets' ground: here the bush burned and was not consumed, as the fifty philosophers burned and were not consumed. The house does not yet know it is hers; it keeps the Bush and the relics of the Law and waits. Above it, on the higher peak, the buried virgin keeps her own vigil in the granite.

stops.name: Mount Sinai, the invention of the relics: the oil
stops.campa: Guided by a vision, the monks climb the great peak and find her: the body of the virgin of Alexandria, incorrupt in the rock, five centuries dead, the holy oil, the myron, welling from her bones. They carry her down to the fortress of the Bush and lay her in a marble chest beside the sanctuary, and the monastery of the Transfiguration becomes, in the mouths of all pilgrims, Saint Catherine's. The head and the left hand keep the church; the oil goes out in phials to the whole world, and with it her name.

stops.name: Mount Sinai, the monk Symeon sets out with the finger
stops.campa: Symeon, monk of Sinai, Sicilian-born, Greek-tongued, guide of pilgrims, is sent west to collect the monastery's alms from the duke of Normandy. As he goes, the legend says, a phalanx detaches itself from one of the virgin's fingers into his keeping: the saint chooses her own courier. He survives Saracen pirates on the Nile and robbers in the passes; the relic rides in his scrip across the whole breadth of the world, from the mountain of the Law toward the rains of Normandy.

stops.name: Rouen, the hill above the city: Sainte-Catherine-du-Mont
stops.campa: On the hill commanding Rouen, Goscelin the viscount founds the abbey of Holy Trinity, and into its altar goes the finger of the virgin of Alexandria and Sinai. The relic swallows the dedication: the abbey becomes Sainte-Catherine-du-Mont and the hill itself the Côte Sainte-Catherine, and Normandy takes her feast, the twenty-fifth of November, into its bones. Miracles gather; pilgrims climb; her legend is preached in Norman French. The philosopher of Alexandria now has a hill over the very city where, four centuries on, a girl who heard her voice will burn.

stops.name: Trier, the Porta Nigra: the courier walled in
stops.campa: His errand done, Symeon of Sinai asks to be buried alive in the east tower of the Porta Nigra, the black Roman gate of Trier, and lives there a recluse until his death on the first day of June, 1035. Within the year, Pope Benedict inscribes him among the saints, among the first men ever canonized by papal decree. So the carrier of Catherine's finger becomes a saint by carrying her: the relay is blessed link by link, and the gate of a dead empire becomes a shrine on the road her cult travels.

stops.name: Domrémy, the garden: Catherine speaks to Joan
stops.campa: In her father's garden at Domrémy, at midday in summer, a peasant girl of thirteen hears a voice from the right, from toward the church, in a great light. Saint Michael comes first; then, as he promised, come Saint Catherine and Saint Margaret, crowned with fair crowns, rich and precious, speaking sweetly and low in the French tongue. The virgin of Alexandria, who out-argued fifty philosophers, takes a pupil who cannot read: for four years she counsels Joan, governs her, and prepares her for the king, the siege, and the sword.
stops.quote: When I was thirteen, I had a voice from God to help me to govern myself.
stops.quote_source: Joan of Arc, trial testimony, Rouen, 22 February 1431

stops.name: Sainte-Catherine-de-Fierbois, the chapel in the woods: a sword laid down
stops.campa: In the iron woods of Touraine stands a chapel of Saint Catherine, and the tradition of the place reaches back to Charles Martel: returning from breaking the Saracens between Tours and Poitiers, the Hammer lays his sword behind the altar as an ex-voto to the virgin of the wheel. Centuries of soldiers follow his example; freed prisoners hang their chains on her walls. Under the altar-stone, in the earth, one blade with five crosses settles into its rust and begins to wait. It knows how long. Seven hundred years.
